notes.text: I'm going to start by calling get_mission to pull up the mission details.

I'm working out what six unknowns the test drops need to reveal: impact point, fall time, whether each drop lands in smoke, and the wind at aircraft altitude. The wind at aircraft altitude is the key quantity, and drops at several altitudes should show how the wind shifts and turns with height, while fall time adds drag information.

I'm weighing whether to test-drop at varying altitudes, since a drop inside the smoke column would pick up updraft. I'll release the first test drop at 100 m, heading 90, speed 60, from (-300, 0), far enough from the smoke that it should measure wind and drag without updraft.

I'm checking the wind at 100 m, speed 6.2 toward 32°, against a fall time of 7.11 s. Without drag, the fall from 100 m would take only about 4.52 s, so drag must be slowing the descent noticeably. I'm considering whether quadratic drag limits the vertical velocity to a terminal speed.

I'm working out the horizontal motion now: releasing at 60 m/s east against a 6.2 m/s wind, quadratic drag would strip off the relative velocity very quickly, so the load would settle near wind speed within about a second. I'm weighing whether to fit the drag coefficient with a simulation, since there are too many unknowns to solve by hand.

I'm weighing whether to fit the wind and drag parameters by running simulations, since there are too many unknowns to solve by hand. Measuring the wind directly at test-drop altitudes would show how it shifts with height, and the fall time should mostly pin down the drag.

I'm planning the next test drops: one at 30 m and one at 150 m, to measure wind and fall time at each altitude. Once I have winds at three heights, the shear and veer should be clear, and then I'll run drops through the smoke to estimate the updraft.

I'm treating the wind at 100 m as settled from the first drop, so drag will come from the fall times and the updraft from the smoke drops. That leaves seven drops to use after the next ones. Next I'll run a test drop at 30 m.

I'm working out the wind shear exponent from the two speeds, 4.4 at 30 m and 6.2 at 100 m, which gives about 0.28. I'm also setting up a veer model where direction changes linearly with height, anchored at 54° at 30 m and 32° at 100 m.

The veer comes out around -31° per 100 m, though with a 4° direction noise that's roughly -31 ± 8. The 4.4 m/s reading at 30 m is also noisy, so the 0.28 shear estimate is only good to about ±0.1. I'm also working out the fall times: 3.29 s from 30 m, with free fall alone giving about 2.47 s, and 7.11 s from 100 m. Next I want to fit drag by comparing predictions against the observations, starting with a drag value of 0.05.

I'm checking the sign of the discrepancy: if dt is predicted minus observed, then at test 1 the prediction would be about 8.56 and at test 2 about 3.52. That would mean the model needs more drag to fall slower.

I'm now weighing drag values: lower drag should shorten the horizontal lag but lengthen the fall, so I'll try 0.03 first, then check the horizontal result against 0.035.

Trying a drag of about 0.027 looks promising, since the first test's slope points there. The second test gives a different zero, around 0.032, so the two estimates don't agree yet.

The wind may be skewing the horizontal misses too, since a 4° direction error alone could shift the lateral result by several meters. I'll run a third calibration drop from 150 m to pin down the wind veer, shear, and drag together.

I'm comparing the wind readings at each height: 6.3 at 24° at 150, 6.2 at 32° at 100, and 4.4 at 54° at 30. Fitting a power law to the speeds gives an exponent around 0.22 across the full range and about 0.28 between 30 and 100, so Iit, roughly 6.2.
